summary:
Ingushetia stands under Russia's national framework: legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned since 2023, the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and national government advisories explicitly warn LGBT travellers against travel to Russia.

Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia and lists Ingushetia among the republics with frequent terrorist attacks, together with Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai. The advisory records surveillance of foreign nationals and states that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, their allies and their families have been attacked, harassed and abused. It notes that since January 2024 organisations advocating on 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as extremist, and that the Ministry of Interior requires special permission to enter certain areas.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He attests that conditions in the region have deteriorated year on year.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Ingushetia, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic regional campaigns against LGBT+ people from 2017 to 2024, and records that the 2023 extremist designation exposes LGBT+ activity to two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising, with violence spreading beyond the region.
tangentialFactors:
At national level, Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the preceding two years.

The tempo of enforcement after the designation is documented: The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as a second-class citizen after the extremist designation.

Ingushetia's situation is generally cited in the sources in relation to its neighbour Chechnya rather than on its own terms. The Home Office note treats the North Caucasus as a single category of heightened persecution risk, and the Canadian advisory lists Ingushetia with Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai on security grounds without differentiating among them.

Physical coercion against transgender people in Russia is documented at national level: BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The UK Home Office note states that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ingushetia face the same national statutes that bind visitors: since 2023 the law has prohibited gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, and the extremist designation exposes LGBT+ organising to two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years. The propaganda law applies to private as well as public speech in practice, and the administrative code provides detention of up to 15 days.

North Caucasus SOS describes a pattern in which even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, with conditions deteriorating year on year. The Home Office documents systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people by regional authorities from 2017 to 2024.

The Ministry of Interior requires special permission to enter certain areas within Ingushetia, a restriction that applies to residents as well as to outsiders, and Global Affairs Canada records surveillance of foreign nationals in the republic.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not resolve how many extremism-related convictions, propaganda-law cases or raids have been recorded within Ingushetia specifically; the national totals cited apply to Russia as a whole and are not disaggregated by republic.

The Canadian advisory does not enumerate which administrative areas within Ingushetia require Ministry of Interior permission to enter, and does not state the penalty for entering them without it.

Whether the documented foreigner penalties of arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation have been applied to LGBT+ visitors inside Ingushetia itself is not sourced here. Likewise, no source documents a conversion-therapy incident, a detention death or a club raid within Ingushetia; the cases cited in the sources occurred in Moscow, St Petersburg and Novosibirsk.
